results.summary: Patients with VP shunts have a 5-10% risk of shunt-related CNS infection over the lifetime of the device. Recurrent community-acquired meningitis in shunted patients may occur via hematogenous seeding or contiguous spread rather than direct shunt colonization.
results.title: Recurrent bacterial meningitis in adults with CSF shunts: risk factors and management

results.summary: Pneumococcal meningitis remains the most common and most severe form of bacterial meningitis in adults. Mortality ranges from 15-30%. Patients with prior CNS insults, CSF leaks, or shunts are at increased risk. Dexamethasone adjunctive therapy before or with first dose of antibiotics reduces mortality and neurological sequelae.
results.title: Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis in adults: clinical features and outcomes in the post-vaccination era

results.summary: Adults with CSF leaks or cochlear implants are considered at high risk for pneumococcal disease. Vaccination with PCV20 or PCV15 followed by PPSV23 is recommended. Patients with history of invasive pneumococcal disease should be vaccinated regardless of prior vaccination status.
results.title: Pneumococcal vaccination in high-risk adults: ACIP recommendations update

alternatives: No alternative corticosteroid is recommended; dexamethasone is the standard adjunctive therapy for bacterial meningitis based on IDSA guidelines

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Consult neurosurgery for evaluation of shunt patency and possible externalisation or replacement.

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis.
No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

differential.key_features: Shunt infection typically subacute with low-virulence organism (CoNS, Cutibacterium); shunt tap of reservoir can confirm

Typically in severely immunocompromised host; cryptococcal antigen and India ink exclude

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.
Shunt-associated meningitis must be distinguished from community-acquired bacterial meningitis; coagulase-negative staphylococci and Cutibacterium acnes are the dominant shunt organisms.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Pneumococcal meningitis can occur in shunted patients and must still be covered with vancomycin + ceftriaxone; shunt evaluation proceeds in parallel.
red_herrings.data_point: Chronic VP shunt raising concern for shunt-related infection rather than community-acquired meningitis
red_herrings.intended_effect: Narrow empiric coverage to shunt organisms (CoNS) and delay broader community-acquired coverage.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Ricardo Fuentes is a 38-year-old right-handed man who was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after his wife found him increasingly confused and febrile at home. He has a significant past medical history of neonatal pneumococcal meningitis complicated by hydrocephalus requiring ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement in infancy, with a single shunt revision during adolescence. He has a residual mild left-sided spastic hemiparesis but is functionally independent in all activities of daily living and works full-time as a warehouse logistics supervisor. Yesterday morning, approximately 18 hours before presentation, the patient developed a frontal headache that he initially attributed to his chronic tension headaches. He took his usual ibuprofen without relief. By the afternoon, his wife noticed he felt warm and took his temperature, recording 38.6 degrees Celsius. He complained of worsening neck stiffness that he described as different from his usual headaches, specifically localized to the posterior neck and exacerbated by bending forward. He took acetaminophen and went to lie down in a dark room, complaining that the living room lights were causing intense pain. Overnight, his condition deteriorated rapidly. His wife heard him moaning and found him curled on his side, drenched in sweat, and mumbling incoherently. He was unable to recognize their daughter and became agitated when she tried to sit him up. He vomited three times between midnight and early morning. By 05:00 this morning, he was barely responsive to verbal commands. His wife called 911 when she was unable to rouse him from bed. Paramedics recorded a temperature of 39.9 degrees Celsius en route and noted significant neck rigidity during assessment. His wife reports no recent sick contacts with meningitis, no recent dental procedures, and no trauma to the head or shunt site. She notes he had a mild upper respiratory infection with nasal congestion approximately ten days ago that resolved on its own. She is unsure of his pneumococcal vaccination status but believes he received childhood vaccinations. There has been no seizure activity witnessed, no new rashes, and no recent changes in shunt function.
